name: The Unlikely History of Bengaluru
description:
Bengaluru was not built in a day. 
This lecture explores the discoveries, encounters, and historical connections that shaped the city as it stands today, drawing on the book Bengaluru: The Comprehensive History to the Dawn of Independence. Most accounts begin in 1537, with Kempe Gowda, but what was already in motion before he arrived? 
The city’s creation was the outcome of thousands of years of unfolding history. By 1537, the ground had been set: first by the geology that shaped the Deccan Plateau, then by the geography that determined its trade routes, and finally by the people, kingdoms, merchants, and armies who moved across this landscape. Each left something behind. Together, they created the conditions for a city to emerge. 

Venue: Seminar Halls


A City Made of Countless Consequences

name: Feather Fest 2026 | Day 2
description:
Have you ever seen or heard
A poem as lovely as a bird?
 
A celebration of the wonder and allure of birds, this two-day festival is made for curious minds of all ages. Storytelling sessions, workshops, talks, and competitions invite everyone to peek into the feathered world and let imagination take flight! 
This is the second edition of “Feather Fest”, presented by Early Bird as part of Young Birders’ Month, a nationwide celebration of birds for young people. 
Schedule 
11am – 12:30pm | Observe, Sketch, Record – Building Your Nature Journal (For Ages 9-18) | Library
with Subath Senan & WWF India
Discover the art of bird observation! Combine basic sketching, behaviour tracking, and field notes to create a personal record of nature.
 
1:30pm – 2:30pm | Games Galore (For Ages 10-13) | Library
with Early Bird Team
Test your memory by matching birds by habitat and food, pick up fun facts, and learn calls of common birds around us. Try to survive as a bird in the Bird Survivor and Life Cycle game.
 
3pm – 4pm | Chirpy Tales – Storytime for children and parents (For Ages 6+) | Library
with Vikram Sridhar
Spread your wings and travel across Bangalore with a storyteller who learnt about Karnataka’s lesser-known birds by waking up early on weekends, running behind a car, climbing a tree, and more. From Black Kites and Indian Rollers to Great White Pelicans, the journey crosses lakes, trees, and bushes. There are new names to learn and a little more of our ecosystem to know!
 
4pm – 6pm | Moving Feathers – Learn More about Birds through Dance & Movement (For Ages 4-8) | Amphitheatre
with Veena Basavarajaiah
Through body movement, children embody different bird behaviours and discover more about our feathered friends, building curiosity and appreciation along the way. Parents are welcome to accompany and watch. Comfortable clothes that allow free movement are best. Get ready to flap, hop, and glide!  
5pm – 6:30pm | A Pocketful of Birds – A Zine-making Workshop (For Ages 10-13) | Library
with Mohit Mahato
This session explores the world of birds through drawing, observation, and visual storytelling. Children turn their observations, thoughts, and experiences into a small handmade zine (booklet), using simple techniques and plenty of room to experiment. No experience in drawing or zine-making is needed. What story will you tell?
 
5:30pm – 6:30pm | A Life Among Birds – Fifty Years of Watching and Wonder (For Ages 14+) | Gallery
with S.Subramanya & Garima Bhatia
A veteran ornithologist looks back on the journeys and stories that shaped a lifelong career with birds, from tracking migrations to retracing the historic bird survey of Mysore State by Salim Ali. Drawing on decades of research and fieldwork, the conversation reveals how scientists study birds, solve mysteries, and uncover connections between birds and the world around them. Birds are fascinating in themselves, but the questions they lead to can be even more intriguing.
 
Across the Weekend | 11am – 7pm 
Let’s Go Birding through Philately | Board Room
Step into a world where birdwatching meets philately in this unique exhibition curated by passionate stamp collector Ramu M. Srinivasa. Featuring a selection from his vast collection, the exhibit showcases bird species across various global themes and taxonomy. The exhibition includes postal materials from the 18th century onwards. 
Measure your Wingspan | Second Floor Foyer
Wingspan is the distance from fingertip to fingertip with your arms stretched out; and it’s the same for birds! To find yours, stretch your arms in a T and compare to that of birds found around Bangalore.
 
Where Islands Take Flight – A Photo Exhibition | Second Floor Foyer
Across 836 islands and islets, the Andaman and Nicobar archipelago is home to 28 endemic bird species found nowhere else in the world. This exhibition features photographs of endemics, from the Nicobar megapode as it stirs at dawn to the Nicobar scops owl as its bright yellow eyes glow at night. Each bird is a small story of how life adapts to island homes, and a reminder of why such fragile places deserve protection. This exhibit is curated by Roundglass Sustain, an initiative of the Roundglass Foundation dedicated to raising awareness and supporting conservation in India’s natural world through evocative, science-backed storytelling.
 
Wings of Wonder – An Exhibition on Raptors | First Floor Foyer
Eagles, kites, falcons, and owls sit at the top of the food chain, and their presence signals a healthy ecosystem. Protecting raptors helps safeguard many other species too. This exhibition by WWF-India opens a window onto the magnificent world of these hunters of the sky, and shows why their conservation matters to every living thing beneath their wings.
 
Flights of Imagination – An Art Exhibition | First Floor Foyer
Young bird lovers from across the country take flight with creativity in this vibrant showcase of the best entries from a national art competition. Hand-made artworks by children aged 11 to 16 celebrate the beauty and diversity of India’s migratory birds, seen through youthful eyes. Each piece carries a little of the journey those birds make, and a lot of the imagination of the artists who painted them. 
Feather Fest Photo Booth | First Floor Foyer
A cheerful corner for festival memories, whether posing solo or with family and friends. Bird-inspired outfits are always in the spirit of the day, and a table of fun bird masks beside the booth adds a flutter of feathers to any look. Strike a pose, show off your best avian style, and let your colours shine!

description:
Based on the book The Unartificial Leader, this discussion asks what humans must hold onto as machines grow more capable. Drawing on interviews with CEOs, founders, and next-generation leaders, the authors argue that intelligence and wisdom are not the same thing. 
The book offers six imperatives, from adaptive resilience to moral judgement, as a framework for leading with clarity in an AI-augmented world: not a rejection of technology, but an argument for deepening human maturity alongside it. Where does your agency sit as you embrace AI?

name: Bengaluru Jatre 2026
description:
Bengaluru Jatre is a Government of Karnataka initiative, led by the Chief Minister and spearheaded by Bengaluru Development Minister Shri Krishna Byre Gowda, with support from city government agencies. 
Many People. Multiple Cultures. One City. 
Across Karnataka, every village and town has its Oora Habba or Jatre, a joyous celebration that brings people of all ages and backgrounds together around life, culture, food, traditions and community. Even when everyday life is full of challenges, a Jatre creates an opportunity to pause, celebrate, connect and find joy together. Bengaluru Jatre brings this spirit to our city. It is envisioned as an annual, city-wide celebration through which Bengaluru comes together to celebrate itself, its people, neighbourhoods, cultures, food, institutions, creativity, history and shared civic identity. 
BIC is happy to be part of the Bengaluru Jatre. 
Schedule 
The Sacred and the Erotic in India Art | Annapurna Garimella
Dec 4-6 | Lectures
The erotic is a resource and artists in India have used it to charge their work with power. Over the course of 3 lectures, art historian Annapurna Garimella will explore how the erotic is creative power in visual and built art, how artists connect it to the sacred and what this connection has made possible. The lectures will be given in English with some Telugu and Hindi poetry included. Each lecture will be approximately a 1 hour presentation with 30 minutes for Q & A. 
Mast Mahila Mandali | Shilpi Gulati, Anjum Shaikh & Sheetal Nawle
Dec 5 | 11:30AM | Screening
Ten women from the eastern suburbs of Mumbai sign up for a filmmaking workshop. Not even knowing where the record button is, they plunge into a messy, immersive process of making a film together. Stealing time away from family responsibilities and daily chores, they turn the camera on themselves. They capture life of the city’s working-class, while talking about husbands, murders, toilets, and everything in between. Evolved from an 18-month process in co-creation, Mast Mahila Mandali is a riotous, plotless, genre-bending documentary about how women labour, love, and claim joy in everyday life.
RSVP here 
Cradle to Grave: Welfare in India | Reetika Khera & Aakar Patel
Dec 5 | 6:30PM | Discussion
Based on the book Freebies or Rights, this discussion examines how social policy actually shapes everyday life: from school meals and the Public Distribution System to maternity benefits and the rural employment guarantee. Is state-provided support simply a set of “freebies” or is it the right that makes a dignified life possible?
RSVP here 
Cultivating Organisational Longevity | Subramanian Kalpathi, Pranay Jivrajka, Vishal Talreja & Aruna Gopakumar
Dec 6 | 6:00PM | Discussion
Modern workplaces pursue growth, agility and performance, yet many unintentionally create conditions that exhaust their people and weaken their capacity to endure. Burnout, toxic cultures, unsustainable ways of working, outdated work models and depleted leaders can reinforce one another, gradually shortening an organisation’s healthy lifespan. This event will examine what current research reveals about burnout, workplace culture and sustainable performance.
RSVP here 
Remaking the Indian Citizen | Yamini Aiyar
Dec 6 | 6:30PM | Lecture
This lecture examines how the democratic boundaries of citizenship in India are shifting, from voting to welfare delivery, asking what the changes mean for the constitutional promise of equal citizenship. It makes the case that routine bureaucratic processes are being used to create a new hierarchy of citizenship, reshaping what it means to be an Indian citizen. Who counts as a citizen? Who decides? 
Smart Machines, Wise Leaders | Swati Apte, Garima Deveshwar Bahl & Shrikant Karwa
Dec 7 | 6:30PM | Discussion
Based on the book The Unartificial Leader, this discussion asks what humans must hold onto as machines grow more capable. Drawing on interviews with CEOs, founders, and next-generation leaders, the authors argue that intelligence and wisdom are not the same thing.
RSVP here 
Bangalore at a Crossroads | Supriya Baily
Dec 8 | 6:30PM | Lecture
In this talk, Supriya Baily explores one of India’s most dynamic cities, Bangalore, through the eyes of a group of women who grew up and went to school together in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Through the stories of school girls in what used to be one of India’s most progressive city, Bangalore Girls reveals how the freedom women once enjoyed has been eroded by the rising tide of right-wing nationalism, misogyny, and religious fundamentalism. 
Art, Madness and Memory | Maitreyee B. Chowdhury & Shamya Dasgupta
Dec 9 | 6:30PM | Discussion
An epistolary novel set in 1969, takes into account the fact that two geniuses, film maker Ritwik Ghatak and Poet Binoy Majumdar find themselves within the same mental asylum. As they discuss their lives, secrets are revealed, dark truths brought to light, and a play is performed. What happens next? 
Six Degrees of Infatuation | Geeta Chandran
Dec 10 | 7:00PM | Performance
Six Degrees of Infatuation, a solo performance by Geeta Chandran, explores the varied dimensions of infatuation, love and adoration that spans the realms of both the divine and the human, drawing from sources as varied as Sanskrit poetry, Vernacular verses, the Ramayana and the vast cornucopia of Indian devotional poetry.

name: The Quiet Storm
description:
This classical piano recital travels through Russian, Polish, and German Romanticism. The performance moves from the intricate counterpoint of Taneyev, through the deeply personal and poetic world of Chopin, to the extraordinary emotional landscape of Schumann, contrasting intimacy and intensity along the way. Is there beauty to be found within the storms the human spirit endures? 
The evening opens in Moscow with Sergei Taneyev, teacher of Rachmaninov and Scriabin. His Prelude and Fugue, written in memory of his lifelong nurse, travels from grief to fierce resolve. Next comes Poland and Chopin, where the storm grows still: two Nocturnes of quiet beauty, then a Scherzo full of wit, play, and sudden flashes of fire. The journey ends in Germany with Robert Schumann, whose music never rests. His moods change from moment to moment, torn between passion and dream, struggle and tenderness.

name: Cultivating Organisational Longevity
description:
This panel discussion looks at what keeps an organisation, and the people within it, healthy, relevant, and effective over time. Modern workplaces pursue growth, agility, and performance, yet burnout, toxic cultures, and unsustainable ways of working can quietly shorten an organisation’s life. Can ambition coexist with care? 
The event begins with an overview of current research on burnout, workplace culture, and sustainable performance, followed by an introduction to the book Heal the Workplace and its RENEW framework for building healthier organisations. The panel consists of practitioners from organisational development, psychotherapy, social entrepreneurship, healthcare innovation, and business-building. They will consider how leaders can support recovery and honest conversation, and how organisations can grow while caring for their people.

name: Rediscovering the Hometown
description:
Shillong is a historical landscape, not only a natural one. 
Based on the book Hometown: Shillong in the World, this conversation examines the city’s layered past to illuminate larger questions of identity, modernity, and belonging in contemporary India, followed by an audience Q&A. What is there to know about Shillong beyond its hills? 
The session takes a deep dive into a small city that began as a British hill station, later became the capital of Assam, and is now the capital of Meghalaya. It follows nostalgia for imagined utopias, the aspirations and confusions of the city’s young, its music scene, its politics and violence, and the growth of both evangelical religion and consumerist desire. Combining thorough research with rigorous reporting, the book skilfully maps the lives and histories that have shaped Shillong. 
Venue: Library

name: In Search of the Snow Leopard
description:
Wildlife researcher Munib Khanyari and artist Nirupa Rao discuss their new book, The Lost Snow Leopard: A Himalayan Adventure, in conversation with conservationist and scientist Charudutt (Charu) Mishra, who brings with him three decades of experience in the field, across High Asia. 
The book commemorates the first ever estimation of snow leopards in Jammu & Kashmir led by Munib, Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi and their colleagues from the Nature Conservation Foundation, in collaboration with the J&K Wildlife Department. The survey helped ‘find’ the region’s snow leopards; decades of regional conflict had made them exceptionally difficult to study, and effectively ‘lost’ to science. Playing on this allusion, The Lost Snow Leopard celebrates Munib’s landmark research, transforming it into an illustrated work of narrative fiction that can be shared with a wider audience of all age groups. 
Munib and Charu share fascinating, firsthand experience of tracking and conserving snow leopards in some of the world’s most challenging terrains, while Nirupa gives us a behind-the-scenes look into combining science and storytelling in the making of the book, and her artistic process. 
Venue: Auditorium

ಅಪೂರ್ವ ಮಹಾಕಾವ್ಯವಾದ ಮಹಾಭಾರತವು ಜೀವನದ ನಾನಾ ಆಯಾಮಗಳನ್ನು ಶೋದಿಸಲು ಪ್ರೇರೇಪಿಸುವ ಚಿಂತನೆಗಳನ್ನು ತನ್ನ ಒಡಲೊಳಗೆ ಹುದುಗಿಸಿಕೊಂಡಿದೆ. ಸಂಸ್ಕೃತ ಮತ್ತು ಕನ್ನಡ ಪಠ್ಯಗಳ ಆಳವಾದ ಪರಿಚಯವಿರುವ ಅಪೂರ್ವ ವಿದ್ವಾಂಸ ತೋಳ್ಪಾಡಿಯವರು ಮಹಾಭಾರತದ ಇಂಥ ಕೆಲವು ಚಿಂತನೆಗಳ ಕುರಿತ ವಿಚಾರಗಳನ್ನು ಈ ಉಪನ್ಯಾಸದಲ್ಲಿ ಹಂಚಿಕೊಳ್ಳಲಿದ್ದಾರೆ.

description:

From hornbills with giant beaks to owlets with enormous eyes, every bird becomes a cartoon character with its own personality. No drawing experience needed, just curiosity. Come ready to spread your creative wings! 
11:30am – 12:30pm | Bird Banter – Bioacoustics, Filmmaking and a Shared Love of Birds (For Ages 14+) | Gallery
with Sugandhi Gadadhar, Chiti Arvind & Suhel Quader
A free-flowing conversation between a wildlife filmmaker, an ecologist, and a scientist and educator, united by a deep love of birds and nature. What is it about birds that keeps them listening, watching, and coming back? 
2pm – 3:30pm | Feathers and Colors – Early Bird Art Room (For All Ages) | Library
Early Bird Join-the-Dots worksheets turn bird identification into art! Connect the numbered dots, colour in each outline, and discover features like beak shapes, crests, tail lengths, and markings, making local species easy to spot and remember. This self-guided colouring activity comes with all supplies provided. Which bird will you reveal first?

with Krishna Murthy, Samira Agnihotri, Mittal Gala & Deepa Mohan
Can you whistle like a magpie robin or call like a shikra? Budding birders, talented mimics, and bird lovers take the stage in a fun, interactive competition celebrating attentive listening, keen observation, and the joy of copying the melodies of the wild. Who will sound most like the real thing?

with Roli Agrawal
Children learn to fold different origami birds, uncover fun facts about their feathered friends, and put together a personalised collection of paper birds to take home as a keepsake. A little creativity, a little nature, and lots of paper folding!

Birds of Bangalore | Gallery (Only on Nov 28)

A city’s ecological richness, the exhibition suggests, is as much a measure of its quality as its architecture and infrastructure. This exhibition features photographs of endemics, from the Nicobar megapode as it stirs at dawn to the Nicobar scops owl as its bright yellow eyes glow at night. Each bird is a small story of how life adapts to island homes, and a reminder of why such fragile places deserve protection. This exhibit is curated by Roundglass Sustain, an initiative of the Roundglass Foundation dedicated to raising awareness and supporting conservation in India’s natural world through evocative, science-backed storytelling.
 
Wings of Wonder – An Exhibition on Raptors | First Floor Foyer
Eagles, kites, falcons, and owls sit at the top of the food chain, and their presence signals a healthy ecosystem. Protecting raptors helps safeguard many other species too. This exhibition by WWF-India opens a window onto the magnificent world of these hunters of the sky, and shows why their conservation matters to every living thing beneath their wings.
 
Flights of Imagination – An Art Exhibition | First Floor Foyer
Young bird lovers from across the country take flight with creativity in this vibrant showcase of the best entries from a national art competition. Hand-made artworks by children aged 11 to 16 celebrate the beauty and diversity of India’s migratory birds, seen through youthful eyes. Each piece carries a little of the journey those birds make, and a lot of the imagination of the artists who painted them. 
Feather Fest Photo Booth | First Floor Foyer
A cheerful corner for festival memories, whether posing solo or with family and friends. Bird-inspired outfits are always in the spirit of the day, and a table of fun bird masks beside the booth adds a flutter of feathers to any look. Strike a pose, show off your best avian style, and let your colours shine!

name: What's All the Song-and-Dance About?
description:
This event explores the emergence of Bharatanatyam in the early twentieth century, told on stage through conversation, music, and dance. Who brought this art into modernity, gesture by gesture? 
Generations of women from professional dance communities sustained the practice, but are rarely remembered today. Based on the book From the Corner of Her Eye: The Many Histories of Bharatanatyam, the conversation shows Bharatanatyam to be a modern form that is also a refashioning of the dance that directly preceded it.

name: Raatri- The Whispers of Night
description:
A Bharatnatyam performance celebrating night, which is both sensual and formidable. As dusk gathers, Radha, adorned with stars, goes to meet her beloved. She becomes night itself: seductress, confidante, and witness. 
The piece opens in starlight and fragrance, with the senses awakened and the god of love invited. In the embrace, Radha’s adornments dissolve, and she asks Krishna to dress her once more. When sleep brings dreams of war and death, and the stillness of the night is broken by the approach of change. A keeper of secrets and a harbinger of loss, the night is both lover and landscape in this performance.

name: The German Musical Legacy
description:
This piano recital celebrates the German musical legacy through the works of Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms, with a special interlude by Claude Debussy. The pianist approaches each piece as a painter might a canvas, creating art through melody and rhythm. 
The programme moves from some of Bach’s and Schumann’s most emblematic piano pieces to Debussy’s “Reflections in the Water” and Beethoven’s deeply expressive Piano Sonata in E major, Op. 109. After a Christmas piece by Liszt, the evening culminates in Brahms’s dazzling Paganini Variations, Op. 35 (Book I).
